description: Project Hail Mary is a 5-member Computer Science & Engineering team building RIMLIGHT for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. We combine NASA LOLA elevation models with JPL SPICE ephemerides to visualize real-time 360° terrain horizons, solar illumination windows, and direct-to-Earth communication overlaps for lunar south pole missions. (Pre-formed team of 5: Youssef, Michael, Lydia, Tia, and Kerolos).
summary: At the lunar South Pole, the Sun never rises above ~1.54° and there is no atmosphere, so landing meters off-target inside a crater rim means total darkness and lost Earth radio contact. RIMLIGHT is an interactive, physics-backed Lunar Landing Site Navigator that lets mission planners, engineers, and students inspect any coordinate south of 80°S on a 60 FPS 3D Moon Globe and 2D Polar Stereographic Map. Powered by NASA LOLA 80 m/pixel topography and NAIF SPICE DE440 ephemerides, RIMLIGHT computes exact sunlit hours, Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows, longest continuous night, minimum battery sizing, a 30-day animated 360° horizon panorama, solar mast trade-offs (2–50 m), 1 m boulder shadows, and NASA Artemis III 4-rule eligibility—validated against Gläser et al. (2014) and Mazarico et al. (2011).
details:
What RIMLIGHT Does

RIMLIGHT transforms complex lunar South Pole topography and orbital mechanics into instant, actionable landing decisions. Users can click any curated NASA/ESA site (such as Connecting Ridge, Shackleton Rim, Shackleton Floor, or Mons Mouton) or any custom coordinate south of 80°S to evaluate power survival, Earth communications, and terrain slope.

How It Works (3-Stage Physics Pipeline)

1. Stage 1 — Ephemeris (SPICE): Computes high-precision Sun and Earth topocentric vectors across 315,576 time steps using NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (naif0012.tls, de440.bsp, moon_pa_de440_200625.bpc, moon_de440_250416.tf, pck00011.tpc).

2. Stage 2 — Terrain Horizon Raycasting: Samples NASA PGDA Product 90 LOLA South Pole DEM (LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ.TIF, 80 m/pixel) across 360 azimuths to build each site's exact terrain horizon mask and 100 m ground slope.

3. Stage 3 — Mission & Artemis III Engine: Calculates sunlit hours, Earth DTE contact (accounting for ±7° lunar libration), longest dark period, battery capacity for configurable 100–200 W loads, mast height trade-offs (2 m, 5 m, 10 m, 20 m, 50 m), 1 m boulder shadow lengths, nearby better-spot search (150–1500 m), and NASA Artemis III 4-rule eligibility (Earth ≥ 25%, Sun ≥ 5%, Slope < 10°, Lat ≤ −84°).

Tech Stack & Validation

- Frontend: React, Vite, Three.js (4K albedo/normal maps + LOLA relief cap + live Earth DTE beacon), Leaflet (L.CRS.Simple), proj4js — hosted on Vercel.

- Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SpiceyPy, Rasterio, PyProj — hosted on Railway with 53 passing pytest unit tests.

- Validation: Cross-checked against Gläser et al. (2014) on Connecting Ridge (-89.4667°, -136.6667°; 92.27% sunlit at 2 m mast, 95.65% at 10 m) and Mazarico et al. (2011) for Shackleton Floor (0% PSR).

- Source Code (MIT License): https://github.com/lydiasalib/NASA-Space-Apps-2026
dataRefs: NASA PGDA Product 90 (LOLA South Pole DEM)
